journal_name: International Journal of Software Tools for Technology Transfer

abstracts.abstract: Traditional software verification approaches rely on either explicit-state model checking or static analysis techniques that operate independently. This paper introduces a Unified Verification Theory (UVT), a novel theoretical framework that bridges the gap between these two dominant paradigms by reformulating verification problems as constraint satisfaction over abstract domains. The core insight of UVT is that both model checking state exploration and static analysis abstraction can be unified under a single semantic foundation based on Kleene's fixpoint theory with domain-theoretic constraints. We formally prove that UVT subsumes existing approaches as special cases while enabling new verification capabilities that were previously impossible within either framework alone. The framework introduces the concept of constraint-bounded verification, which provides theoretical guarantees for termination while maintaining soundness over infinite-state systems. We demonstrate the theoretical implications through several theorems establishing connections between previously disparate verification techniques. This paradigm shift opens new research directions for verification tool development, as the unified semantics suggests that tool implementations can be generalized to operate across multiple verification paradigms simultaneously. The theoretical contribution establishes UVT as a foundational framework for next-generation verification methodologies.

Bounded model checking (BMC) suffers from exponential state space growth that limits its applicability to large-scale industrial software systems. This paper presents Symmetric Path Unrolling (SPU), a significant theoretical advancement that exploits structural symmetries in program control flow to dramatically reduce the search space during BMC. The core contribution is a formal characterization of path symmetry based on program structure analysis, which identifies equivalence classes of execution paths that exhibit identical verification-relevant behavior. We prove that analyzing only one representative path per equivalence class yields sound and complete verification results. The theoretical framework extends traditional BMC semantics by incorporating a symmetry-aware unrolling strategy that systematically avoids redundant exploration while maintaining full coverage guarantees. Additionally, we introduce symmetry-aware interpolation operators that enable more effective Craig interpolation in symmetric contexts, improving the precision of inductive invariant generation. Our analysis establishes complexity bounds showing that SPU reduces the worst-case time complexity from O(n!) to O(n^k) where k depends on the program's symmetry degree. These theoretical results provide the foundation for implementing practical verification tools with substantially improved scalability.

Existing verification toolchains suffer from fragmented architectures where disparate tools operate in isolation, requiring significant manual effort for integration and losing synergy between complementary analyses. This paper presents MetaVerif: An Integrated Verification Workbench, a novel tool architecture that fundamentally rethinks verification tool design through a unified intermediate representation layer. MetaVerif introduces three core architectural innovations: (1) a universal verification IR (V-IR) that provides semantic-preserving representations for programs, properties, and analysis results across different formalisms; (2) a dynamic tool composition framework that enables arbitrary verification tools to be combined through semantic-aware adapters without modification to existing tools; and (3) an intelligent verification planner that automatically selects and sequences analysis techniques based on program characteristics and verification objectives. The system implements a plugin architecture supporting extension through standardized interfaces, with currently integrated tools including CBMC, SPARK, Frama-C, and CBMC. Evaluation on industrial benchmarks demonstrates that MetaVerif enables verification scenarios previously impractical due to tool limitations, with the integrated approach discovering defects missed by individual tools while reducing overall verification time through parallel analysis strategies.

Large-scale static analysis of industrial codebases remains impractical due to the prohibitive cost of repeated full analyses during iterative development. This paper introduces IncrementalSat, a significantly improved static analysis engine designed for continuous integration environments where analysis must complete within practical CI/CD time constraints. IncrementalSat implements a novel function-level incremental analysis architecture that tracks dependencies between analysis results at multiple granularities. The system design centers on three key improvements: (1) a hierarchical result caching mechanism operating at function, module, and system levels with semantic-aware invalidation; (2) a change impact analysis module that precisely determines which cached results remain valid after code modifications; and (3) an adaptive analysis precision selector that automatically adjusts analysis depth based on available time budgets and verification priorities. The implementation extends the Frama-C platform with these incremental capabilities while maintaining compatibility with existing plugins. Experimental evaluation on real-world industrial projects totaling over two million lines of code demonstrates that IncrementalSat achieves up to two orders of magnitude speedup compared to full re-analysis, with negligible precision loss. The tool has been successfully deployed in production CI pipelines, reducing average analysis time from hours to minutes.
